descriptionChirho: The primary sense of בַּעַל as one who owns, possesses, or has mastery over property, animals, or objects. This is the most frequent use, covering ownership of an ox (Exod 21:28-36, 22:8-15), a pit (Exod 21:34), a field (Exod 22:5), a house, or goods. Includes the construct chain בַּעַל + noun ('owner of X') and pronominal forms (בְּעָלָיו 'its owner'). The Covenant Code in Exodus uses this sense extensively for property law. Glosses show ownership semantics: arb صاحِب 'owner,' deu Besitzer/Eigentümer, fra propriétaire, spa dueño, hin मालिक/स्वामी, kor 주인.

labelChirho: lord, ruler, citizen-lord of a city
descriptionChirho: בַּעֲלֵי + city name: the lords, rulers, or leading citizens of a city, denoting civic authority rather than mere ownership. Dominant in the Judges narrative for the lords of Shechem (בַּעֲלֵי שְׁכֶם, Judg 9:2-51, occurring ~15 times), and also for the lords of Jericho (Josh 24:11), the lords of Keilah (1 Sam 23:11-12), and the lords of high places (Num 21:28). These are the ruling oligarchy or citizen-assembly of Canaanite city-states. The plural construct בַּעֲלֵי is characteristic. Glosses: arb سَادَة 'lords,' deu Herren, eng 'lords of,' spa señores de, kor 주인들.

בַּעַל as 'husband,' reflecting the ancient Near Eastern concept of the husband as lord/master of the household. Used of Abimelech's relationship to Sarah (Gen 20:3 בְּעוּלַת בָּעַל 'married to a husband'), in laws about a married woman's vows (Num 30), of the husband of the Proverbs 31 woman (Prov 31:11, 23, 28), in Esther 1:17, 20 regarding wives honoring their husbands, and of Joel's marital metaphor (Joel 1:8). Glosses distinguish this from the general 'owner' sense: arb زَوْج 'spouse,' deu Ehemann, fra mari, spa esposo/marido, hin पति, kor 남편.

labelChirho: one characterized by a quality (idiomatic בַּעַל + attribute)
descriptionChirho: Idiomatic use of בַּעַל in construct with an abstract quality or physical attribute, meaning 'one who has/possesses' that characteristic. Functions like English 'man of' or 'one having.' Examples include בַּעַל כְּנָפַיִם 'one having wings' (Prov 1:17, referring to a bird), בַּעַל שִׁנַּיִם 'one having teeth/tusks' (Isa 41:15, of a threshing sledge). This is a productive idiomatic construction rather than a separate lexeme, but its semantic function is distinct from literal ownership. Glosses show attributive meaning: arb ذِي 'possessing,' eng 'having,' spa 'dueño/ave,' kor 가진 자.

בַּעֲלֵי בְּרִית: 'lords of a covenant,' i.e. allies or confederates bound by treaty. Attested in Gen 14:13 where Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner are described as בַּעֲלֵי בְּרִית אַבְרָם 'allies of Abram.' The term denotes partners in a mutual defense pact or covenant relationship. The German gloss Bundesgenossen 'confederates' captures this well. This is semantically distinct from general 'lords of a city' because the relationship is defined by covenant rather than civic authority. Glosses: deu Bundesgenossen, eng 'possessors of [covenant],' spa aliados, hin सहभगि, kor 동맹자들.

בַּעַל used of a designated official or officer in a bureaucratic/military context. In Jer 37:13, בַּעַל פְּקִדֻת denotes an 'officer of the guard' or 'chief inspector' at the Benjamin Gate. This extends the 'master/lord' concept into formal administrative titles. The term designates someone holding a specific post of authority, distinct from general property ownership or civic lordship. Glosses: arb رَئِيسُ 'chief,' eng 'officer of,' spa 'jefe de,' hin अध्यक्ष 'chairman/head.' A specialized administrative usage attested rarely.
